analysis.one_liner: Raises the cap on deducting state and local taxes to $80,000 through 2030.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a floor vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the $10,000 cap on the federal deduction for state and local taxes to $80,000 for tax years 2021 through 2030, then drop it back to $10,000 for 2031. The cap was part of the 2017 tax law and falls hardest on homeowners in high-tax states like New Jersey and New York. The bill would mainly benefit upper-income households who itemize deductions and pay large state tax bills. It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income taxpayers in high-tax states—New Jersey, New York, California, Illinois—who pay large state property and income taxes and itemize deductions. The $80,000 cap would let households with six-figure state tax bills deduct far more, saving tens of thousands of dollars a year. Only those who itemize benefit; the vast majority of taxpayers who take the standard deduction would get nothing.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the state and local tax deduction cap from $10,000 to $80,000 ($40,000 for married filing separately) for tax years 2021 through 2030, letting wealthy homeowners in high-tax states deduct far more of their property and income taxes.
Reverts to the $10,000 cap in 2031, so the benefit is a temporary, ten-year windfall rather than a permanent change.

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury and all federal taxpayers. The tax revenue lost would have to be made up by borrowing or by other taxes, since no offset is in the bill. The benefit is concentrated on high-income itemizers, so the general public effectively subsidizes it.
analysis.who_pays_short: All federal taxpayers through lost revenue

drawbacks.text: Roughly all of the benefit would go to the top earners: only itemizers with very large state and local tax bills would gain, and households earning well into six figures would get nothing or nearly nothing.
The bill contains no revenue offset, so it would add to federal deficits for ten years to fund a deduction that overwhelmingly helps the wealthy.

Sunsetting back to $10,000 in 2031 makes it a budget-gimmick shaped windfall rather than a lasting reform, and the anti-avoidance guidance it authorizes suggests Congress expected taxpayers to try to game the timing rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax relief is real but aimed almost entirely at upper-income itemizers in a handful of high-tax states, and the lost revenue would be borne by everyone through deficits or future taxes. For the typical household, the bill would do nothing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never held a hearing or sent it to the floor, and it died there when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced November 18, 2021 by Rep. Chris Smith (R-NJ) and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The committee took no further action—no markup, no vote—before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody changed status quo: the current $10,000 SALT cap stayed in place, and federal revenue was not spent on a tax cut concentrated on high earners in a few states.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for votes or recorded positions; the sponsor is a Republican from a high-tax state where the SALT cap is politically costly.

industries.note: Would have gained up to $70,000 more in deductible state and local taxes, a direct tax cut for affluent homeowners, but the bill failed.
